t: Last Substring in Lexicographical Order — Two-Pointer Duel
o: We must return the lexicographically largest substring of `s`. Since every substring is a suffix of some prefix, the answer is always the suffix starting at the best index — so we only need to find the **starting index** of the maximum suffix. For "abab", comparing candidate starts: 'b' beats 'a', and between the two 'b' positions (1 and 3), "bab" > "b", giving index 1 → "bab". For "leetcode", the largest character is 't' at index 4, and "tcode" is maximal. With n up to 4·10^5, an O(n²) comparison of all candidates is too slow in the worst case (e.g. "aaaa...a"), so we need a linear or near-linear method.
k: The answer is the suffix of s with the largest starting index under lexicographic order; we only need that index.
The two-pointer duel advances by the length of the matched prefix, guaranteeing O(n) total work since each pointer skips forward permanently.
The problem is equivalent to finding the last Lyndon factor's start via Duval's algorithm.

a.i: Track the best starting index found so far. For each new index i, compare s[i:] against s[best:] character by character; if it is strictly larger, update best. This is simple but each comparison can cost O(n), giving O(n²) worst case (e.g., all same characters).
s: For each i from 1 to n-1, compare s[i:] with s[best:] using a helper that walks characters until they differ or a string ends.
If s[i:] > s[best:], set best = i.
a.t: O(n²) worst case — each of the n candidates may require an O(n) character-by-character comparison.
a.sp: O(1) extra space besides the output slice.

a.i: Maintain two candidate starting indices i < j and duel them: walk k forward while the characters match. When they differ, the smaller side loses entirely — crucially, every start between i and i+k also loses to the winner's corresponding position, so we can jump i past the whole matched region. Each step permanently advances at least one pointer, so total work is linear.
s: Set i = 0 (current best) and j = 1 (challenger), k = 0 (matched prefix length).
While j + k < n: if s[i+k] == s[j+k], increment k and continue.
If s[j+k] > s[i+k], the challenger wins: set i = max(i + k + 1, j), then j = i + 1, k = 0.
Otherwise the incumbent wins: set j = j + k + 1, k = 0.
a.t: O(n) — after comparing k matched characters, one pointer jumps forward by at least k+1, so total advancement across all iterations is bounded by n.
a.sp: O(1) extra space besides the returned substring.

w: In an interview, present the brute force briefly to establish correctness, then derive the two-pointer duel: the key argument is that when s[i..i+k] ties s[j..j+k] and s[j+k] differs, *all* starts in [i, i+k] are dominated, justifying the jump. Pitfalls: forgetting the `max(i + k + 1, j)` guard (needed when the tie run overlaps the old i), off-by-one on resetting k, and handling single-character strings (loop never runs, returns s itself). Edge cases: all identical characters (answer is the whole string minus first char... actually the full string), strictly increasing strings (last character), and long runs of equal letters where the linear bound matters most. Follow-ups: relate this to Duval's Lyndon factorization (the answer is the start of the last Lyndon factor), or solve the general 'k-th largest suffix' with suffix arrays.
